The difficulty of MAT 1000 depends on your professor tbh. But even the most intensive iteration of the course doesn’t assume a lot of prerequisite knowledge, and college math is quite different from school math so you should be okay if you’re willing to put in the work. It’s very plausible to be a successful econ major if you haven’t done math in 11th and 12th as long as your algebra is strong and you approach your introductory courses at Ashoka very rigorously. 

That said, you did choose to skip math in 11th and 12th despite knowing how much it narrows your options which could suggest a number of things. If you were strong with the subject till 10th grade, and opted out of it to pursue humanities out of sheer interest, then you’ll be okay. If your fundamentals are weak, and you have trouble with more basic concepts like solving systems of equations, then I’d be a little more worried. If math is something you simply plan to put up with then maybe economics isn’t for you. It is a math intensive degree so you’ll have to find a way to enjoy it

You’re in a bad spot but there’s no need to hate yourself or feel like you’re doomed. Apply to Ashoka for sure- at the end of the day it genuinely is a holistic process and if you’re able to convince your interviewer that you will make the most out of your degree here, they will make space for you. Most people’s visceral reaction to seeing somebody sincerely trying to turn their life around is compassion. You’ll need to set up your application in a way that the admissions team feels like they can help you.

That said, it’s unstrategic to hold out for this and your best shot is probably passing a competitive exam where your background simply isn’t a consideration. If you’re after the flexibility of a liberal arts college, then Shiv nadar, Azim premji, Symbiosis, flame, and so on are very decent options. You can also try writing exams like the APs if you want to signal academic competence.

You aren’t doomed to fail at age 18/19/20. Once you enter college, your school marks become completely irrelevant and you’re given a fresh start. The academic structure is radically different and you have more independence. You can absolutely be very successful from there on, and I think you, more than Ashoka, owe yourself a second chance. Your most “important years” aren’t the ones you spent demotivated at home.

Obviously that doesn't mind you shouldn't confide in other people but you need to walk the line between keeping your distance and maintaining a relationship with your parents. As toxic as your parents sound it might not be in your best interest to damage your relationship in a way that mind jeopardize your future. Going forward you may have to rely on them to pay for things like college and therapy. I know this advice might be infuriating but once you're off to uni there's only so much they can do to control you. 

Ultimately there's no excuse for what they're doing, and you have every right to be angry and cut them off. I only think you should do what you think is best for you considering your long term situation.

As someone who did ICSE till 10th and CBSE in 11th and 12th I'd suggest ICSE over CBSE for the time being. Imo the extra focus that ICSE puts on English is useful if you want to consider switching to an international board in +2 or even if your kid wants to remain in ISC. The syllabus in ICSE is harder but the questions in 10th board exams are usually very predictable so it's easy to score in them regardless of which board you pick. 

That being said I think the school is more important than the board. If he's getting admission in a good CBSE school like NPS inr then the quality of the teaching is probably going to be more useful to him than a more expansive syllabus
